clue.text: Fortify Mosley? Confound it! That's what always happens to me

definitions.text: That's what always happens to me

indicators.note: an exclamation of annoyance that also orders the preceding names to be confounded, that is jumbled up

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry about the fascist Mosley, ending in a weary sigh at one's own bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confound it!' reads as a curse but is the anagram signal on FORTIFY MOSLEY. Oswald Mosley led the British fascists in the 1930s.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom spoken resignedly when the same misfortune strikes yet again, as if it summed up one's whole history.

clue.text: It reverts to seed with awfully hot and gaudy flier

indicators.note: to revert is to turn back, so the word It is read backwards

parts.note: a germ is a seed or embryo from which something grows

indicators.note: awfully suggests something badly done, so these letters are put into a disordered arrangement

explanation.surface: Something going back to seed alongside a showy flying creature that is terribly hot.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a brightly patterned moth species, a showy insect flier; the name also belongs to a vintage biplane.

clue.text: It's capital to love a lover

parts.note: Rome is the capital city of Italy
love is nil in tennis scoring, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A remark that it is splendid to love someone who loves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' looks like the old slang for 'excellent', but it is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's young hero of Verona gave his name to any ardent wooer, so it serves as a generic term for a lover.

clue.text: Transport books put together

definitions.meaning: an old word for a bus, a public passenger vehicle
a single volume collecting several works, such as an author's novels

explanation.surface: Vehicles and bound volumes assembled together.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a passenger bus and a collected edition of several books in one volume.

clue.text: Corn collected on road? Got it wrong

indicators.note: in a down answer, on means the corn piece is placed below, after, the road

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI in crosswords
a stook is a group of sheaves of corn stood together in a field

explanation.surface: A farmer leaves gathered grain on the highway and realises the error.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is Britain's main motorway, from London to Leeds; crosswords read the figure 1 as the letter I. A stook is a stand of sheaves drying in a field.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb meaning erred or misjudged, here in the past tense like the definition's 'got it wrong'.

clue.text: Unction etc is commonplace in a girl

indicators.note: in places the word for commonplace inside the word for a girl

parts.note: lass is a northern British word for a girl
trite means hackneyed or commonplace

explanation.surface: Anointing ceremonies described as nothing special for some young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Catholic sacraments given to the dying, including anointing with oil, which is what unction means.

clue.text: Far from pleased at policeman being promoted?

parts.note: a fed is American slang for an FBI agent, a federal officer
someone promoted has moved up

explanation.surface: Someone is unhappy at a police officer's advancement in rank.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom for being thoroughly fed to the back teeth, fed to the point of annoyance and boredom.

clue.text: Cheat outrageously holding high cards that may be worn out

indicators.note: holding means the jumbled letters surround the cards placed within them
behaving outrageously means acting wildly, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the king is one of the high-ranking court cards in a pack
the jack, or knave, is another high court card

explanation.surface: A card sharp cheats wildly, keeping top cards up a sleeve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outrageously' makes HACET from its fodder, which 'holding' wraps round the two court cards. 'worn out' means worn outdoors, not threadbare.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweed jacket designed for riding, so it is clothing put on to go outdoors; 'worn out' puns on 'tattered'.

clue.text: Parrots talking back to very old-fashioned 15 in very long words

indicators.note: talking signals that the word for the birds is sounded out, not spelt

parts.note: Polly is the traditional name for a pet parrot, so parrots in general are Pollies

indicators.note: back to tells us the word for very is written backwards

parts.note: bally is a dated euphemistic intensifier meaning very or bloody
the comic at 15 down has the first name Les

explanation.surface: Talking birds, set against a dated comedian, come out with lengthy vocabulary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back to' turns BALLY into YLLAB. LES is the first name of the answer to 15 down, the comedian Les Dawson.
explanation.definitionFit: A word with many syllables is by definition a long one, the opposite of a monosyllable.

clue.text: Disputes with watcher about people taking time

indicators.note: about means the watcher's name goes around the other pieces

parts.note: Argus was the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth set to keep watch
men stands for people in general

explanation.surface: Quarrels arise with a lookout over people who dawdle.
explanation.walkthrough: Argus Panoptes, the giant with a hundred eyes, guarded Io for Hera.
explanation.definitionFit: A plural noun meaning quarrels or disagreements, exactly as the definition 'Disputes' does as a noun.

clue.text: Loner maybe put on like this outside

indicators.note: outside means the phrase for like this goes around the word for put on

parts.note: so means in this manner, like this
to add is to put something on top, as in adding to a pile

explanation.surface: A recluse perhaps dresses this way in the open air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on' and 'outside' read like dressing up to go out; they are the pieces and the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a pitiable, socially inept person, and a loner is one example of such a person.

clue.text: Ship's company with slow start heard on tableland

indicators.note: heard tells us the word is said aloud, here drawn out

parts.note: a ship's company is its crew, spoken with its first sound dragged out into an extra syllable

explanation.surface: A vessel's personnel, slow to get going, can be made out on a high plateau.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'crew' slowly at the start, 'ca-roo', and it sounds like the answer, which is a dry South African upland.
explanation.definitionFit: A semi-desert high inland plateau of South Africa, a raised flat region, which is what tableland means.

clue.text: I go back and knock hard, entering by 1, say

indicators.note: entering means these pieces go inside the word by

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back tells us the word go is written in reverse

parts.note: to rap is to knock sharply
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone retreats and bangs firmly, coming into a house beside the first entry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns GO into OG; then I, OG, RAP and H go 'entering' BY. The answer to 1 across is a phrase for one's life story.
explanation.definitionFit: A life story is an account of someone's life, and 'say' signals the 1 across phrase is an example.

clue.text: Name for lots of strips of pasta

parts.note: oodles is informal for lots, a great quantity

explanation.surface: A label given to many ribbons of pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: Long thin ribbons of dough, as in Chinese or Italian cooking; the plural matches 'strips'.

clue.text: Comic bird interrupting instruction

indicators.note: interrupting means the bird breaks into the middle of the word for instruction

parts.note: a lesson is a period of instruction
a daw, or jackdaw, is a small crow

explanation.surface: A funny bird breaks into a teaching session.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Dawson was a British comedian of the 1970s and 80s, famous for his deadpan mother-in-law jokes and off-key piano playing.
explanation.definitionFit: He was a famous British stand-up comedian, so he is an instance of a comic.

clue.text: Sky, it may be, keeps companion of unsophisticated taste

indicators.note: keeps means the rearranged letters hold the abbreviation inside them
may be suggests the letters of Sky it could be something else, so they are rearranged

parts.note: CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A satellite channel, perhaps, retains a partner with low-brow preferences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' rearranges SKY IT into KITSY, which 'keeps' CH: KITS-CH-Y. Sky is a British satellite television company.
explanation.definitionFit: Describing showy, tasteless art or decor that appeals to undiscerning taste, an adjective like the definition.

clue.text: Money order on the debit side with squares

indicators.note: in a down answer, on puts the debit piece below, after, the money order

parts.note: a cheque is a written order to a bank to pay money
being in the red means owing money, the debit side of an account

explanation.surface: A banker's draft drawn on an account in deficit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with squares' reads like a mathematical phrase; it describes a pattern, as on a draughtboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Patterned with alternating coloured squares like a draughtboard, an adjective meaning marked with squares.

clue.text: One wearing long pants produced 13s of 23 down

parts.note: long johns are woollen underpants reaching the ankles, shortened here to johns
a garment one is wearing is on

explanation.surface: Somebody in long underwear wrote the lives of the poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' is the subject of both halves: someone with johns on. Samuel Johnson wrote Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Johnson wrote a celebrated set of short life stories of English poets, so he is the one who produced them.

clue.text: One odd record, unknown coinage

indicators.note: odd suggests the word One is put into a strange arrangement

parts.note: a log is a written record, as a ship's log
Y is one of the letters used for an unknown quantity in algebra

explanation.surface: A single strange entry with an unfamiliar new expression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges ONE into NEO.
explanation.definitionFit: The coining of new words; coinage likewise means inventing new expressions.

clue.text: Body part for important person who produced 13 of 18

indicators.note: part means only a portion of the word Body is kept, its last two letters dropped

parts.note: a swell is a grand or important person

explanation.surface: Asking which bit of the anatomy stands for someone of rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body part' reads as anatomy, but it asks for a piece of the word itself. James Boswell wrote the famous Life of Samuel Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: James Boswell wrote the classic life story of Samuel Johnson, so he is its author.

clue.text: Digs organised during prohibition, which is ominous

indicators.note: during places the rearranged letters inside the word for prohibition

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition

indicators.note: organised means the letters of Digs are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Lodgings being tidied up while something is forbidden: not a good omen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organised' rearranges DIGS into DSIG, which goes 'during' BAN. 'Digs' is British slang for rented lodgings.
explanation.definitionFit: A portent of trouble ahead, the kind of omen that bodes ill, matching 'which is ominous'.

clue.text: Paleface in political group reported — do I bother?

indicators.note: reported means the word for the group is taken by how it sounds

parts.note: a caucus is a group within a political party

indicators.note: a bother is a fuss or commotion, so these two words are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A white man among the politicians, apparently, wondering whether to bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do I bother?' reads as a weary question; 'bother' as a noun (a commotion) rearranges DO I into OID.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated anthropological term for the white-skinned race, and paleface was the old term for a white person in Westerns.

clue.text: Superior meal with no starter

indicators.note: with no starter means the word for the meal loses its first letter

parts.note: supper is an evening meal

explanation.surface: A grand dinner served without a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' looks like a first course of the meal, which fits the surface; it is the opening letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective meaning higher in rank or position, as in the upper house or upper class.

clue.text: Absolutely sound?

definitions.meaning: used as an adverb meaning utterly or completely
a verb meaning to measure the depth of water with a weighted line

explanation.surface: A question whether something is entirely reliable.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means utterly, as an adverb, and as a verb means to measure depth with a lead line.

clue.text: All fools, they say, take one drug among others

indicators.note: among places the single drug inside the others

parts.note: pots stands for other drugs, pot being slang for cannabis
E is the slang abbreviation for one ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: Everybody's an idiot, people claim, swallowing a pill with their friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' is a link. The definition quotes a saying that writers of verse are all fools.
explanation.definitionFit: A rueful saying holds that writers of verse are foolish dreamers, so the definition names them by reputation.

clue.text: Shows former NCOs

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
POs are petty officers, non-commissioned officers in the navy

explanation.surface: Ex-sergeants are put on display.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of a short word for an exhibition or exposition, a public show such as a world's fair.

clue.text: Oil producer in riot with levee being destroyed

indicators.note: being destroyed means the letters are broken up and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: An oil refinery hit in a riot as the river embankment is demolished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oil producer' suggests a refinery or rig; it is a tree yielding olive oil. A levee is a riverbank embankment.
explanation.definitionFit: The tree yields olives, which are pressed for oil, so it literally produces oil.

clue.text: Peg to refuse and Daddy's on a roll

parts.note: bran is the husk left after milling grain, a kind of refuse

indicators.note: on a roll suggests tumbling, so the letters of Daddy's on a are rolled around into a new order

explanation.surface: A hook for rubbish, and father is doing well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roll' rearranges DADDYS ON A into DYANDSODA. A peg is an old Anglo-Indian word for a measure of spirits with soda.
explanation.definitionFit: An old Anglo-Indian word for a drink of spirits topped up with fizzy water, especially this mix.
